In deep learning, the geometric complexity of a model refers to the intricacy of the decision boundaries it establishes. This paper investigates the geometric complexity of deep learning models, specifically focusing on the impact of data augmentation on the geometric complexity of a model trained on a dataset. We demonstrate that the geometric complexity of a model trained on a data-augmented dataset is at most the geometric complexity of a model trained on the original dataset, plus the geometric complexity of the data augmentation method. This finding is significant as it provides a theoretical basis for understanding the role of data augmentation in deep learning models.

We have developed a comprehensive and user-friendly tool for analyzing the Wilson coefficients of rare $b \to s$ transitions, which are influenced by new physics. This tool, known as WilsonPlots, is designed to be easily accessible and can be utilized by both experts and beginners. It is available for free at https://github.com/leptonflavour/WilsonPlots.

Recent advancements in transformer-based language models have significantly enhanced the performance of automated essay scoring systems. Building on this progress, we introduce a novel approach that leverages pre-trained models like BERT and RoBERTa to develop a more efficient scoring system. Our method involves fine-tuning these models on a smaller dataset, which we then use to train a lightweight linear classifier. This approach yields a scoring system that achieves a correlation of 0.89 with human evaluations, while requiring only 10% of the computational resources needed by a comparable model.

We demonstrate that any toric model based on marginal independence can be transformed into a toric model with a specific structure by applying a linear coordinate change. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the equivalence classes of these models and the equivalence classes of a specific type of directed graph.

A key aspect of social mobility is the role of higher education, which is often seen as a pathway for individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds to achieve upward mobility. This study examines the relationship between higher education and intergenerational mobility in a specific context, using data from the 2010 census in Brazil. The analysis reveals that the impact of higher education on mobility is not uniform across different socioeconomic groups, with the effect being more pronounced for individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. The study also finds that the impact of higher education on mobility is not solely due to the type of degree obtained, but rather influenced by the socioeconomic status of the individual's parents.

The symmetry of the wavefunction under parity has a significant impact on the exchange statistics of identical particles in quantum mechanics. This effect is explored in the context of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, where the parity symmetry of the wavefunction leads to a specific relationship between the wavefunction's behavior under parity and its exchange properties.

A decentralized cryptocurrency system, Delegated RingCT, is proposed to enhance the efficiency of blockchain technology. This system combines the concepts of ring signatures and delegated proof of stake, allowing for a more efficient and secure blockchain. By utilizing a delegated ring signature scheme, the Delegated RingCT system enables a more efficient blockchain, while also maintaining the security and privacy of transactions. This paper presents the Delegated RingCT system, along with its security and privacy properties, and demonstrates its efficiency through a detailed analysis.
We expand the range of linear systems solvable by existing solvers for undirected Laplacian matrices, and we also develop a new solver for a broader class of matrices.

The LHCb experiment at the LHC has conducted a search for the simultaneous creation of three massive gauge bosons in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, with a dataset of 900 inverse femtobarns. The analysis focuses on the fully hadronic decay mode of the bosons, with the most significant findings being the production of three W bosons and three Z bosons, with observed significance levels of 2.8 and 2.5 standard deviations, respectively. The results are compared to the Standard Model predictions and the limits on anomalous triple gauge couplings are also presented.

Hebrew text has been the subject of various NLP tasks, including word segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the Hebrew language, its writing system, and the NLP tasks that have been developed for it.

We examine the isometric dimension reduction of subsets within the L_p space, specifically focusing on the isometric embedding of the maximum of n functions into a lower-dimensional L_p space. Our research reveals that for any subset of n functions in L_p, there exists a way to isometrically embed it into a lower-dimensional L_p space with a dimension of O(n^{1-1/p} log^2 n). This finding is a direct consequence of a more general theorem that provides a lower bound for the Euclidean distortion of subsets within the L_p space.

In the field of artificial neural networks, catastrophic forgetting poses a significant challenge to continual learning, where models tend to lose previously acquired knowledge when trained on new data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the concept of a "virtual teacher" to guide the learning process. By incorporating a "student" network that mimics the behavior of the teacher, we can effectively prevent the loss of previously learned information. Our method is demonstrated to be effective in various continual learning tasks, including classification and regression, and can be easily applied to existing neural network architectures.

This research investigates the impact of degree-degree correlations on the performance of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes in a binary erasure channel. We derive a formula for the probability of a degree-$d$ variable node being connected to a degree-$d'$ check node, given a specific degree distribution. We then demonstrate that degree-degree correlations can be minimized by optimizing the degree distribution, and we provide a method for achieving this optimization. We also examine the effect of degree-degree correlations on the threshold of LDPC codes and show that the threshold can be improved by minimizing these correlations.

This paper presents an enhanced model predictive safety filter (MPSF) that leverages a discrete-time system model to ensure safety in the presence of disturbances. By incorporating a discrete-time system model, the proposed method offers a more accurate representation of the system's behavior, resulting in improved performance and reduced computational complexity. The resulting formulation is a convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved in real-time. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a numerical example.

The effectiveness of quantum key distribution (QKD) is heavily reliant on the security of the devices used, but imperfections in these devices can be exploited by eavesdroppers. This research explores the potential of using a specific type of device, known as a quantum switch, to enhance the security of QKD systems. By utilizing a quantum switch, the system can be made to function as if it were composed of two separate channels, each with its own unique properties. This allows for the creation of a more secure QKD system, even when the devices used are imperfect.

Recent advancements in large language models have demonstrated the effectiveness of in-context learning, which allows models to adapt to new tasks without additional training. Our research investigates the impact of pretraining data sources on in-context learning performance. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of various language models, including GPT-3, GPT-J, and GPT-Neo, across multiple datasets and found that models pre-trained on diverse data sources exhibit improved in-context learning capabilities. Furthermore, we discovered that models with a larger vocabulary size tend to perform better in in-context learning tasks.

The interplay between galaxy clusters and their surrounding environments is a key area of study in astrophysics. To understand this relationship, researchers have developed a model that simulates the growth and evolution of cold gas clouds within galaxy clusters. This model, which incorporates the effects of galaxy cluster mergers, has been used to investigate the impact of these events on the distribution of cold gas within galaxy clusters. The results show that the model can reproduce observed trends in the distribution of cold gas within galaxy clusters, including the relationship between the mass of the galaxy cluster and the fraction of cold gas. The model also suggests that the distribution of cold gas within galaxy clusters is influenced by the frequency and intensity of galaxy cluster mergers.

The study of CP violation in the Standard Model is a crucial tool for testing its predictions. The LHCb experiment has made significant progress in this area, particularly in the measurement of CP violation in the decay of B0_s to J/psi phi. The LHCb collaboration has also made notable advancements in the measurement of CP violation in the decay of B0 to D0 K0 and in the determination of the CKM angle gamma.

We have developed a novel approach to calculating hard string scattering amplitudes, specifically for open superstring theory. This method is based on a new, efficient formula for the four-point amplitude, which is derived from the original expression by applying a series of transformations. The resulting formula is then used to derive a general expression for the n-point amplitude, which is subsequently applied to derive the hard scattering limit for the n-point amplitude.

In the upcoming mobile networks, machine learning will play a crucial role in predicting and optimizing resource management. This paper presents a novel approach to resource allocation in 5G networks by combining a deep learning-based prediction model with a reinforcement learning-based optimization strategy. The proposed method utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to forecast user data rates and then employs a Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm to optimize resource allocation. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of throughput and fairness.

Zerospeech synthesis systems generate speech from acoustic units called phonemes, 
which are then combined into words and sentences.  This paper introduces a new 
approach to zerospeech synthesis that utilizes phoneme sequences as input, 
employing a novel method to create phoneme representations from raw audio data. 
The phoneme representations are then used to train a phoneme recognition model, 
which is subsequently applied to a phoneme-based speech synthesis system.  The 
results show that this method can produce high-quality speech with a relatively 
small amount of training data.

This research focuses on the motion planning of multi-limbed robots, which is a complex optimization problem that can be solved using a specific approach. By utilizing a particular method, we can transform the problem into a more manageable form, which can then be solved using a specific algorithm. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations involving a two-legged robot, which is capable of walking on uneven terrain.

We establish a fundamental requirement for the physical transformation of quantum states in affine quantum resource theories, which is also a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a resource-preserving quantum channel.

A nonlinear pendulum system is analyzed with parametric excitation and external forces, and its stability is investigated using the method of multiple scales. The results show that the system's stability is influenced by the excitation parameters, and the stability boundaries are determined by the excitation frequency and amplitude.

In this research, we introduce a novel approach called Distributionally Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD) to address the challenge of distributed optimization under uncertain data distributions. Our method combines the benefits of robust optimization and decentralized learning, allowing it to handle both issues simultaneously. We demonstrate that DR-DSGD achieves a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ under specific conditions, and our numerical experiments show that it outperforms traditional DSGD in terms of communication efficiency.

In high-energy nuclear collisions, the energy released is directly related to the number of particles produced. This relationship is explored through the lens of the color glass condensate model, which is used to calculate the energy released in collisions. The model's predictions are compared to experimental data from the RHIC and LHC colliders, specifically focusing on the energy released in collisions and its correlation with particle production. The results show that the model's predictions are consistent with the observed data, particularly in terms of the energy released in collisions and its correlation with particle production. The model's predictions also suggest that the energy released in collisions is directly related to the number of particles produced, which is an important finding for understanding the dynamics of high-energy nuclear collisions.

We've conducted a comprehensive study on the impact of magnetic fields on the development of protostellar jets using 3D simulations. Our research focused on the formation of jets in a magnetized environment, specifically examining the effects of varying magnetic field strengths and mass accretion rates. Our findings indicate that jets can form in a wide range of conditions, but their behavior is significantly influenced by the strength of the magnetic field. Our simulations also reveal that the magnetic field strength affects the mass and velocity of the jets, as well as the presence of outflows and the formation of bow shocks. Our results suggest that the magnetic field strength plays a crucial role in the development of protostellar jets and their interaction with the surrounding environment.

This paper introduces a novel control framework for constrained nonlinear systems, which effectively balances the trade-off between performance and saturation. The proposed approach utilizes a performance safety evaluation function to quantify the system's capacity to maintain performance without entering saturation. A safety filter is then designed to prevent the system from exceeding this capacity, thereby ensuring the system remains within its operational limits. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through simulations of a nonlinear system subject to actuator saturation.

This study examines the oblateness of the Earth and its impact on resonant equilibrium points for objects with a high area-to-mass ratio. The research focuses on the 1:1 resonance, where the object's orbital period matches the Earth's rotation period. The study derives the equations of motion for the object in the rotating frame and identifies the equilibrium points. The results show that the oblateness of the Earth significantly affects the resonant equilibrium points, particularly for objects with a high area-to-mass ratio. The study also provides a numerical analysis of the resonant equilibrium points for different values of the area-to-mass ratio and the oblateness coefficient. The research has implications for the design of future space missions and the understanding of the dynamics of objects in the Earth's vicinity.

We've developed a tight-binding model that incorporates light-matter interaction using the dipole gauge, which is equivalent to the velocity gauge but offers a more intuitive approach. This model is particularly useful for studying the effects of strong light on materials, as it allows for a more straightforward analysis of the dipole response. We've also demonstrated that our model can be used to investigate the behavior of a 2D material under the influence of a strong laser, and that it can be used to study the effects of the laser on the material's electronic structure.

This paper presents a novel method for 3D pose and shape estimation of objects, specifically designed to address the issue of intra-class variability. Our approach utilizes a multi-view learning framework, which incorporates a shared latent space to capture the essential features of objects, thereby enabling the accurate prediction of their 3D poses and shapes. By leveraging a shared latent space, our method can effectively handle the complex variations within object classes, thereby improving the overall performance of 3D pose and shape estimation.

A Cauchy distribution is characterized by two parameters, $\mu$ and $\sigma$, which can be combined into a complex parameter $\zeta = \mu + i\sigma$. This paper derives the maximum likelihood estimator for $\zeta$ in a sample of $n$ independent and identically distributed random variables, and demonstrates that the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal.

Basket trials are a type of clinical study that assesses the efficacy of a new treatment across multiple patient groups with different characteristics. To analyze basket trials, we developed a statistical model that incorporates a shared treatment effect and group-specific variations. This model allows for the estimation of treatment effects and the identification of the most effective patient groups. We also created a Bayesian method to determine the optimal number of patients in each group, considering the uncertainty in treatment effects.

High-precision motion systems are increasingly reliant on advanced control strategies, but conventional designs often fall short due to their inability to account for complex dynamics and uncertainties. To address this limitation, a novel approach is proposed that combines a neural network-based disturbance observer with a model predictive controller. This method enables the prediction of future system behavior and the optimization of control inputs, while also compensating for unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving precise motion control.

We introduce a novel, unsupervised point cloud registration technique that leverages a keypoint detector to identify distinctive features in point clouds. By employing a self-supervised learning approach, our method optimizes the keypoint detector and descriptor extractor using a combination of keypoint matching and descriptor similarity loss functions. Our experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art registration methods, particularly in scenarios involving unaligned keypoint positions.

A group G is said to have property R for all if every twisted conjugacy class within G is finite. This paper demonstrates that the group of automorphisms of a free group of rank n possesses property R for all.

The top quark mass is a crucial factor in determining the stability of the Higgs potential. We have developed a method to calculate the top quark mass in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme using the principle of minimal sensitivity, which involves a specific choice of renormalization scale. This method is then applied to the Standard Model and the Standard Model extended with a singlet scalar, where we find that the top quark mass in the extended model is significantly lower than in the Standard Model.

A novel approach to time-resolved data analysis is introduced, which involves inverting a nonlinear equation to extract a continuous function from noisy data. The method is demonstrated through its application to the analysis of the time-dependent absorption spectrum of a molecular system, specifically the 2D electronic spectrum of a photosynthetic complex.

We have developed a novel approach to calculate the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for mesons, which are essential for understanding the internal structure of mesons. Our method is based on the light-front wave function of mesons, which is derived from the Bethe-Salpeter equation using a specific interaction model. This model is the Brodsky-Huang-Lepage model, which is a widely used interaction model in particle physics. Our results are in good agreement with previous calculations and provide a reliable framework for further research.
This paper investigates the nontriviality of the space $\Sigma^s_\sigma$ for $s\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma\in(0,1)$. We establish that $\Sigma^s_\sigma$ is nontrivial if $s<\frac{\sigma-1}{2}$.

Segmenting unlabeled imaging modalities is a challenging task due to the absence of ground truth data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the inherent characteristics of labeled modalities to facilitate instance segmentation of unlabeled ones. Our method, called Self-Supervised Instance Segmentation (SSIS), utilizes a self-supervised learning technique to create a shared feature space for both labeled and unlabeled modalities. By employing a contrastive learning framework, SSIS aligns the feature representations of unlabeled modalities with those of labeled ones, thereby enabling the transfer of segmentation capabilities. Our experiments demonstrate that SSIS outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness.

A novel Recurrent Neural Network is proposed to generate future video features and predict actions, leveraging the temporal dynamics of actions and the efficiency of end-to-end training. The network's design enables the use of pre-trained CNNs for feature extraction, while also allowing for the incorporation of multiple action recognition models. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through experiments on the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets, yielding state-of-the-art results.

The occurrence of white-light stellar flares on M-dwarf stars has significant implications for the habitability of their planets and the detection of biosignatures. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have developed a new model that simulates the emission spectra of stellar flares. This model is based on the assumption that the energy released during a flare is distributed across different wavelengths according to a power law. By applying this model to observed data, researchers have found that the energy released in the ultraviolet and visible light ranges is significantly higher than previously thought. This finding has important implications for the habitability of planets orbiting M-dwarf stars and the detection of biosignatures.
We establish a connection between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, and demonstrate that a nearly parallel G2 structure is equivalent to the existence of a real Killing spinor.

A linear operator T on a complex Hilbert space is considered C-normal if it satisfies the equation TCCT* = C*T*C*T, where C is a complex number. This paper explores the C-normality of Toeplitz operators on the Dirichlet space, specifically those with symbols that are either real-valued or have a modulus of 1.
We establish a one-to-one correspondence between p-core p'-partitions with a specified number of elements and a particular type of p-quotient, which consists of a p-partition and a set of integers.

This study introduces a novel benchmark for point cloud models, focusing on their ability to handle 3D transformations. We have developed a comprehensive dataset, comprising 100,000 synthetic point clouds, each with a randomly applied 3D transformation. The benchmark categorizes these transformations into three groups: rigid, affine, and projective. We have also evaluated the performance of various point cloud models, including PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, and KPConv, on this benchmark.

In FMCW radar networks, CSMA protocols are commonly used to prevent interference. A key component of these protocols is the clear channel assessment (CCA), which determines whether the channel is clear before transmission. This paper presents a novel CCA method that leverages the characteristics of FMCW radar signals to enhance the accuracy of channel assessment. The proposed approach utilizes the received signal strength (RSS) of the FMCW radar signal to estimate the channel state, thereby reducing the likelihood of false assessments. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulations and experimental results.

We have successfully observed the interaction of entangled photons with a material that exhibits a non-linear response, specifically in the form of a silicon waveguide. Our experiment involved measuring the transmission of entangled photons through the waveguide and found that the transmission probability is influenced by the entanglement of the photons. This effect is observed as a reduction in transmission probability, which is consistent with theoretical predictions.

We examine the complex projective space CP(V), which is a compact, complex manifold composed of complex lines within a complex vector space V. This space is a homogeneous space, and we investigate the existence of a specific type of connection on CP(V), which is a connection with a specific curvature property. This connection is a complex analogue to a connection previously studied in real projective space RP(V).

Temporal knowledge graph reasoning has gained significant attention, with a focus on predicting future events and time intervals. A notable approach involves using a temporal knowledge graph embedding model, which has been shown to be effective in various applications. This paper presents a new method for temporal knowledge graph reasoning that combines a temporal knowledge graph embedding model with a temporal knowledge graph completion task. The proposed approach is evaluated on two datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting future events and time intervals.

The perceptibility of ground sound resulting from a rigid-body impact is investigated. The study reveals that the sound's audibility is influenced by the impact's location, the object's velocity, and the ground's material properties. The findings are supported by experimental data and a theoretical model that accurately predicts the sound's characteristics.

We demonstrate that 'always-type' all-versus-nothing proofs can be established using correlations that are imperfect, thereby challenging the notion that only perfect correlations can yield such proofs. This is achieved by introducing a new criterion for quantum contextuality that is equivalent to the existence of an all-versus-nothing proof.

We introduce a novel approach to create flat bands in a two-dimensional lattice system, which can be achieved through the use of a specific type of boundary condition. This boundary condition is characterized by a set of parameters that can be adjusted to control the system's behavior. The proposed method is applicable to a wide range of systems, including those with itinerant and localized characteristics. The boundary condition is demonstrated to be effective in creating flat bands in a two-dimensional lattice system, which can be used to study the behavior of systems with localized and itinerant characteristics. The proposed method is also shown to be effective in creating flat bands in a two-dimensional lattice system, which can be used to study the behavior of systems with localized and itinerant characteristics.

A hydrogen boride monolayer, featuring a unique honeycomb structure, has been identified as a potential superconductor. Our research reveals that this material exhibits a robust superconducting potential, with a critical temperature of 10.5 K, surpassing that of its parent compound, borophene. Our calculations indicate that the hydrogen boride monolayer possesses a high density of states at the Fermi level, which is primarily composed of hydrogen s-orbitals. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the hydrogen boride monolayer exhibits a high electron-phonon coupling constant of 0.51, which is significantly higher than that of borophene. Our findings suggest that the hydrogen boride monolayer is a promising candidate for the development of high-temperature superconducting materials.

We have developed a new approach to analyze flattened partitions, which are a specific type of partition where each part is a non-increasing sequence of non-negative integers. Our method involves using a generating function to count these flattened partitions, which is then used to derive a formula for the number of such partitions with a given sum. This formula is used to calculate the number of flattened partitions with a given sum, which is shown to be equal to OEIS number A124324.

We establish a new classification of ergodic measures in dynamical systems, specifically those that are 'rigid', which exhibit a unique property of having a limited range of possible behaviors. Our findings demonstrate that any ergodic measure in a system with a specific type of interaction, known as a short-range potential, is classified as 'rigid'.

In highly automated driving systems, redundancy is crucial for fail-operational systems. This paper presents a novel approach to designing redundant fail-operational systems, specifically tailored for automated driving. The proposed method involves a modular architecture that separates the system into a primary and backup module, each with its own distinct functionality. The most accurate representation of Leibnizian calculus is the differential and integral calculus, as outlined in the Acta Commentarii. This paper explores the historical context of Leibniz's calculus, specifically focusing on the Acta Commentarii, and examines the implications of recent scholarship by Mancosu, which argues that Leibniz's calculus is best understood as a geometric framework.

We have developed a novel method to analyze HI intensity mapping data, which allows for the estimation of cosmological parameters using power spectrum multipoles. By applying this method to simulated data, we demonstrate that it can effectively constrain key cosmological parameters, including $\Omega_{\rm m}$, $h$, $\sigma_8$, and $w_0$, with a level of precision comparable to existing analyses.
We establish a connection between the linear independence of a sequence of vectors and the dimension of the vector space they generate.

Recommender systems face a significant challenge due to data sparsity, which hinders their ability to provide accurate recommendations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the relationships between users and items to create a more comprehensive representation of the data. By utilizing a graph-based method, we can capture the underlying structure of the data and improve the accuracy of the recommendations. Our approach is evaluated on a large-scale dataset and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods.

We establish a general framework for asymptotic freeness of random matrices, which encompasses both self-adjoint and non-self-adjoint matrices, as well as matrices with distinct spectral properties. Our approach is based on a novel criterion that can be applied to a broad class of matrix ensembles, including those with varying degrees of self-adjointness.

This paper introduces a novel approach to real-time system monitoring using Metric Interval Temporal Logic, which allows for the expression of complex temporal properties. We develop a monitoring algorithm that can be efficiently executed in a distributed manner, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a case study involving the monitoring of a real-world system.

We examine isospin violation in meson-meson transitions, focusing on the role of electromagnetic interactions. Our analysis reveals that the isospin-violating amplitude for the transition $\eta\to\pi^0\gamma\gamma$ is primarily influenced by the mass difference between up and down quarks, rather than electromagnetic effects.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera, a key component of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, is designed to perform three main tasks: aligning the telescope, measuring the position of celestial objects, and capturing images. This paper outlines the camera's design and operational principles, along with its performance metrics.

We investigate the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, a variant of the Capacitated k-Supplier problem, where we aim to select a subset of facilities and clients to minimize the sum of connection costs and opening costs, while also considering a limited number of excluded clients. We demonstrate that this problem can be solved efficiently using a parameterized approximation scheme based on the number of excluded clients and the number of facility connections per client.

This paper demonstrates that every entire solution of the differential difference equation $f^{(k)}(z+c)^n + P(z)f(z+c)^m + Q(z) = 0$ is a polynomial, where $k, m, n$ are positive integers, $c$ is a non-zero complex number, and $P(z)$, $Q(z)$ are polynomials.

This paper presents a probabilistic algorithm for solving linear systems of polynomial equations with errors, which can be applied to the problem of finding a hidden polynomial of a given degree. The algorithm's efficiency is measured by the number of evaluations required, which is shown to be within a constant factor of the optimal number of evaluations needed for a noise-free version of the problem. The algorithm's performance is also demonstrated to be within a constant factor of the optimal number of evaluations needed for a related problem of finding a polynomial of a given degree.

We have developed a theoretical framework to analyze parity-symmetric photon emissions in quantum systems, specifically those with two-photon and four-photon correlations. Our approach is based on the parity symmetry of the underlying Hamiltonian, which allows us to derive general properties of the emitted photons. We have applied this framework to a model of a quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide, and found that parity-symmetric photon emissions exhibit distinct characteristics, such as the absence of odd-order correlations and the presence of even-order correlations. Our results provide a foundation for the design of parity-symmetric quantum devices and the study of their properties.

A new analytical equation of state for pure alkali metals is proposed, which is based on a specific mathematical expression. This equation of state is capable of accurately predicting the behavior of these metals under extreme conditions, including their compressibility, bulk modulus, and melting points. The equation of state is also capable of accurately modeling the behavior of these metals at both high and low pressures, and it is in excellent agreement with experimental data and theoretical predictions.

The mass spectrum of light vector mesons is examined in the context of chiral imbalance, with the mesons modeled as $q\bar{q}$ bound states. The study reveals that chiral imbalance significantly impacts the mass spectrum, with the $J^{PC}=1^{--}$ state exhibiting a mass decrease and the $J^{PC}=1^{+-}$ state exhibiting a mass increase.

The algorithm is designed to accommodate up to $f$ Byzantine nodes, where $f$ is less than or equal to $n/3$, and it achieves agreement in $O(f)$ rounds. In numerical relativity simulations, solving the Hamiltonian constraint is crucial for accurately modeling matter configurations. A new approach to solving this constraint is presented, which involves a modified version of the standard equation. This modified equation is solved using a combination of iterative methods and a specific numerical technique. The results show that this approach is effective in solving the Hamiltonian constraint for various matter configurations, including those with complex structures.

The JUNO experiment is a large-scale neutrino detector located in China, designed to study the oscillation properties of neutrinos. To achieve this, the experiment will utilize a 20 kiloton liquid scintillator target and a 500 megawatt reactor array. JUNO's primary objective is to precisely measure the neutrino mass ordering and the oscillation parameters $\Delta m^2_{31}$ and $\sin^2\theta_{12}$. Additionally, the experiment will investigate the reactor antineutrino anomaly, solar neutrinos, supernova neutrinos, and geoneutrinos.

Long sequence time-series forecasting is crucial in various fields, including traffic prediction and energy consumption analysis. This paper presents a novel approach, the Long Sequence Transformer (LST), which leverages a transformer-based architecture to tackle the challenge of long sequence forecasting. The LST model is designed to handle long sequences by incorporating a multi-scale attention mechanism and a novel position encoding scheme. The LST model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods.

We have developed a new method for calibrating an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) that utilizes a single image from a spectrograph. This approach is based on the assumption that the ADC's dispersion is linear and that the wavelength calibration is accurate. By analyzing the residual dispersion in the observed spectrum, we can determine the ADC's dispersion coefficient. This method has been tested using data from the Keck/DEIMOS spectrograph and has shown promising results, with a precision of 0.00015 per pixel for the ADC's dispersion coefficient.

We introduce a novel approach to knowledge distillation for ranking models, 
which leverages the insights from a pre-trained teacher model to enhance the 
performance of a smaller student model. Our method is versatile and can be 
applied to various ranking models, including those based on pairwise and listwise 
learning paradigms. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields 
significant improvements in terms of NDCG@10 and MRR metrics, with a notable 
reduction in model size.

We investigate the potential of using a near-zero-frequency component in a network of atomic clocks to detect interactions with ultralight bosonic dark matter. Our research demonstrates that this method can be more sensitive than traditional approaches, which rely on frequency shifts, and that it can be implemented with existing technology.

We examine the inverse problem of determining a Radon measure from its low-frequency Fourier components. This problem is equivalent to a moment problem, and we establish the uniqueness of solutions under specific conditions. Our analysis reveals that uniqueness holds when the measure is supported on a finite number of points, and we provide a method to identify the number of these points. Additionally, we investigate the stability of solutions and show that they are stable when the measure is supported on a finite number of points.

P4, a domain-specific language, enables the programming of programmable switches to process packets. P4 programs are designed to be hardware-agnostic, allowing them to run on various switch architectures. However, the lack of a standardized compilation process for P4 programs has led to the development of multiple compilers, each with its own limitations. This paper introduces a novel approach to compiling P4 programs into a hardware-agnostic intermediate representation, which can then be optimized and compiled into specific hardware architectures.

A novel approach to solving the vector transport equation is presented, utilizing a higher-order function space to achieve a more accurate solution. The method is based on a least-squares formulation, which is then solved using a preconditioned conjugate gradient algorithm. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through numerical experiments, which show that it can achieve a more precise solution with a lower computational cost.

Deep learning has garnered significant attention due to its remarkable performance in various applications, yet it also raises significant ethical concerns. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the ethical implications of deep learning, focusing on key areas such as fairness, privacy, and security. We also highlight the importance of explainability and transparency in deep learning systems, and discuss the potential risks associated with adversarial attacks. By examining these issues, we hope to contribute to the ongoing discourse on the responsible development and deployment of deep learning technologies.

The LHCb experiment has discovered an excited state of the $B_c^+$ particle, specifically the $B_c(2S)^+$, with a mass of 6.908 GeV and a width of 0.045 GeV. This finding is based on the analysis of $B_c^+ \to J/\psi K^+$ decays, which were recorded during 2016-2018. The data collected by the LHCb experiment has allowed for the observation of the $B_c(2S)^+$ state, which is consistent with theoretical predictions.

We introduce a novel class of numerical methods, Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods, which are designed to solve Hamiltonian systems and maintain energy conservation properties. These methods are developed by combining the principles of symplectic Runge-Kutta methods with the concept of boundary value problems. The resulting methods are shown to be capable of achieving arbitrary order accuracy while maintaining the symplectic nature of the solution. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in preserving the symplectic structure of the solution.

We introduce a novel approach to updating groups of layers in neural networks, 
where each group is evaluated by a local critic network. This critic network 
assesses the impact of the group update on the network's performance. The 
critic network is trained using a combination of the group update and the 
network's output, which is then used to guide the update of the group. The 
approach is shown to be effective in improving the performance of neural 
networks, particularly in the context of transfer learning and domain adaptation.

In a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system, we investigate the impact of weak dissipation on non-Wada basins. Our findings reveal that under weak dissipation, these basins become unstable, leading to the emergence of chaotic transients.

We investigate the production of lepton pairs through the interaction of a photon and a Z boson, specifically focusing on the case where the photon is produced via the interference of two virtual photons. This phenomenon can result in significant distances between the production and decay points of the lepton pair, which can be exploited to identify the process. We examine the potential for detecting this process at the LHC and propose a method for identifying it using the lepton's impact parameter.

This paper introduces a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) for human action recognition, which leverages a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture the temporal structure of videos at multiple levels. The HAN model is designed to capture the relationships between frames and segments, and it is capable of identifying the most relevant frames and segments for action understanding. The HAN model is evaluated on the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets, and it achieves state-of-the-art results with a simple architecture.

This study examines the Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole in the presence of a cosmological constant and electric charge. It is demonstrated that a naked singularity can exist if the horizon radius is less than a specific critical value. Furthermore, it is shown that the critical value of the horizon radius is independent of the electric charge.

The universe's star formation process is a fundamental aspect that also encompasses planet formation. To investigate this, researchers have developed a novel approach to analyze the distribution of star-forming regions in the universe. By utilizing a dataset of 10,000 star-forming regions, researchers have found that the distribution of these regions exhibits a fractal pattern, characterized by a specific dimensionality. This dimensionality is found to be consistent across various scales, indicating a self-similar structure in the universe's star-forming regions. Furthermore, researchers have discovered that the distribution of star-forming regions is influenced by the universe's large-scale structure, which is characterized by a specific dimensionality. This finding has significant implications for our understanding of the universe's evolution and the processes that govern star and planet formation.
This paper presents a novel approach to calculating Shannon entropy and mutual information for probability distributions, utilizing the concept of fractional calculus.

This research focuses on modeling semiconductor manufacturing systems using a continuous approach, which is particularly challenging due to the discontinuous nature of the system's velocities. To address this issue, we develop a novel method for solving the resulting Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations by combining a continuous model with a discrete approximation. The discrete model is then used to approximate the value function of the continuous system, which is shown to converge to the true value function as the discretization becomes finer.

A minor security breach can have severe consequences for a company, including financial losses and damage to its reputation. To mitigate these risks, we propose a novel approach to detect and prevent such breaches by analyzing the company's network traffic. Our method involves using a machine learning model to identify anomalies in the traffic, which may indicate a breach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on real-world network traffic data.
We establish a Schreier growth gap for groups acting on trees, which is a key finding in our research.

Animals move for various reasons, such as seeking food, escaping predators, and navigating their environment. To understand the mechanics of this movement, researchers have developed a mathematical model that simulates the motion of a soft, deformable body in a fluid environment. This model, based on the principles of fluid dynamics and elasticity, is used to study the locomotion of soft-bodied organisms, such as worms and octopuses. By applying this model, researchers can gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of animal movement and potentially develop new technologies for soft robotics.

This research focuses on optimizing the power transmission network by minimizing electricity surplus and transmission losses. A novel approach is developed to address this issue, which involves a two-stage optimization process. Initially, the power flow is optimized to minimize losses, and then the electricity surplus is minimized. The proposed method is tested on a 14-bus power system, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.

The application of machine learning and artificial intelligence to scientific research has gained significant traction, with the goal of using measurement data to derive universal physical laws. However, the inherent limitations of data-driven approaches pose a significant challenge, as they are susceptible to inaccuracies and incomplete information. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that combines machine learning with a Bayesian approach to model the underlying physical laws governing the data. This framework enables the integration of prior knowledge and uncertainty quantification, thereby enhancing the reliability of the derived laws.

We have developed a novel method to identify hypothetical long-lived particles that are massive and charged, which are produced in particle collisions and decay into other particles. Our approach leverages the distinct characteristics of these particles, such as their unusual trajectories and energy signatures, to differentiate them from standard model particles. By applying this method to data from the Large Hadron Collider, we have successfully identified a new type of long-lived particle that is consistent with theoretical predictions.

We have developed a novel single-photon source that utilizes a quantum dot integrated into a photonic crystal waveguide, which is connected to a photonic crystal fiber. This setup enables the collection of photons emitted by the quantum dot with high efficiency, resulting in a Purcell factor of 100 and a collection efficiency of 60%. The system's performance is further enhanced by the ability to tune the emission wavelength of the quantum dot, which allows for the generation of indistinguishable photons at 1550 nm.

We have developed a method to analyze the vibrational density of states around the boson peak of a glass using a combination of Raman spectroscopy and a theoretical model. This approach allows us to determine the vibrational density of states in the vicinity of the boson peak, which can then be compared to the vibrational density of states of a liquid. Our results show that the vibrational density of states around the boson peak of a glass is similar to that of a liquid, which is consistent with the idea that the boson peak is a remnant of the liquid's vibrational modes.

The calculation of three-loop electroweak and mixed electroweak-QCD corrections is a complex task, but it is essential for achieving the required precision in particle physics. This paper outlines the methodology for computing these corrections, with a focus on the use of the differential equations method. The approach is demonstrated through the analysis of a specific example, the mass of the W boson, and the results are presented in terms of master integrals.

We introduce a novel approach to analyze the behavior of a random-scattering system, where particles are randomly placed in a system and their interactions with incoming particles are tracked. This method allows us to study the system's response to a steady stream of particles and its long-term behavior. By applying this approach to a specific model, we demonstrate that the system's response can be accurately predicted using a mathematical model that takes into account the system's long-term behavior.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the central region of the Galaxy, 
examining the distribution of gas in the Near and Far Arms. By utilizing a 
novel method, we have identified a significant symmetry between these arms, 
which is evident in the gas distribution patterns. This symmetry is particularly 
pronounced in the central region, where the Near and Far Arms exhibit a 
distinctive "S" shape. Our findings suggest that the Galaxy's central region 
is characterized by a complex interplay of gas dynamics, which may be influenced 
by the presence of a central bar structure.

Optimization methods that prioritize diversity can uncover a broad range of high-quality solutions, whereas other methods typically yield a single optimal solution. This research presents a novel approach to quality diversity optimization, which is based on a new, efficient algorithm that utilizes a graph-based representation of the solution space. The proposed method, called Graph-based Quality Diversity (GQD), is designed to be adaptable to various problem types and can be easily integrated with existing optimization techniques. The results of our experiments demonstrate that GQD outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

We investigate the three-dimensional variant of the Stable Roommates problem, where each participant has preferences for a triplet of other participants. We demonstrate that a stable matching exists in this scenario, provided the preferences adhere to a specific symmetry. This symmetry is equivalent to a symmetric valuation, which we show is a necessary condition for the existence of a stable matching. Additionally, we establish that the problem is NP-complete when the preferences are not symmetric, and we provide a polynomial-time algorithm for solving the problem when the preferences are symmetric.

In two-dimensional materials, valley Hall responses are influenced by static strain, which can be manipulated to control valley Hall currents. We have developed a theoretical framework to investigate the valley Hall response in a strained graphene-like system, which is characterized by a specific type of band structure. Our analysis reveals that the valley Hall response is highly sensitive to the type of band structure, which can be either Dirac or massive. We have also found that the valley Hall response is significantly affected by the presence of a specific type of band structure, which is characterized by a specific type of mass. Our results have important implications for the development of valley Hall devices, which can be used to control valley Hall currents in graphene-like systems.

We introduce a novel concept of a cloud within metric spaces, which is a specific subset of the Gromov--Hausdorff distance space. This cloud is a compact, convex subset of the Gromov--Hausdorff distance space, and we demonstrate that it is a closed subset of the Gromov--Hausdorff distance space.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna operating in the mm-wave range is designed for integration into planar arrays. The patch antenna operates within a 28 GHz frequency band, spanning from 26.5 to 29.5 GHz. The patch antenna is designed with a 100 mm x 100 mm substrate, featuring a 50 ohm microstrip feed line. The patch antenna exhibits a 10 dB return loss bandwidth of 2.5 GHz, and its radiation pattern is characterized by a 12 dBi gain at 28 GHz.

Quantum computation's reliability can be significantly improved by using topological error-correcting codes, which are based on the principles of quantum mechanics. These principles are also applicable to the study of quantum spin systems, which are often used to simulate complex quantum phenomena. In this research, we explore the possibility of using a quantum spin system to implement topological error-correcting codes, specifically the toric code, which is a widely studied code. By utilizing a quantum spin system, we can potentially create a more efficient and scalable quantum computer.

Quantum metrology leverages quantum mechanics to enhance measurement precision, particularly in interferometry. This technique can be applied to measure the phase shift of a light beam passing through a medium, such as a gas, with high accuracy. By utilizing a specific quantum state, researchers have demonstrated that the phase sensitivity can be significantly improved, with the potential to surpass the standard quantum limit. This improvement is achieved by optimizing the quantum state and the measurement process, with the result being a more precise measurement of the phase shift.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has studied the production of high-momentum hadrons in Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV, comparing them to p+p collisions at the same energy. The results show that in Au+Au collisions, hadrons with a significant portion of the quark's momentum are suppressed more than those with a smaller fraction. This suppression is observed to be consistent with the pattern seen in p+p collisions, indicating that the effect is not influenced by the number of participating nucleons. The findings also reveal that the suppression of these high-momentum hadrons is more pronounced than that of the most commonly produced particles, such as pions, kaons, and protons.

In digital-analog quantum computing, we investigate the optimal connectivity of qubits for simulating spinless fermions, focusing on the efficiency of the Jordan-Wigner transformation. We demonstrate that a linear qubit arrangement is the most efficient for this purpose, and we analyze the performance of this arrangement in the context of the Fermi-Hubbard model.

We introduce a novel method for initializing networks with rich representations, 
which significantly enhances the efficiency of optimization and the quality of 
generalization. Our approach involves pre-training a network on a large dataset, 
followed by the extraction of a compact, yet informative, representation that can 
be used to initialize the network. This representation is then optimized using 
standard techniques, resulting in improved performance and faster convergence. 
Our method is versatile and can be applied to various types of networks, including 
convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Our experiments 
demonstrate that our method outperforms existing initialization techniques, 
resulting in state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

Achieving precise light focusing through cloudy substances is a significant challenge in various applications, including medical treatments and imaging. A new approach has been developed to enhance the accuracy of light focusing in such media by utilizing a machine learning algorithm. This method involves training a neural network to predict the optimal phase pattern for a spatial light modulator, which is then used to compensate for the distortions caused by the turbid media. The results show that this approach can significantly improve the accuracy of light focusing in cloudy substances, with a notable increase in the intensity of the focused light.

A new approach to policy evaluation is introduced, which leverages data from the testing distribution during the training phase to achieve more efficient results. The proposed method, known as the two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimator, is demonstrated to be asymptotically unbiased and consistent under specific conditions. The effectiveness of this method is further validated through a series of experiments conducted in both simulated and real-world environments.

This research investigates the performance of CMOS sensors with a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, comparing it to standard epitaxial materials. The study focuses on the impact of substrate resistivity on hit-detection efficiency and charge collection, specifically examining sensors with a 100-micron thickness and 100-micron pixel size. The results indicate that the high-resistivity Czochralski substrate offers improved hit-detection efficiency and charge collection, particularly at lower bias voltages.

The primary goal of exoplanet imaging is to detect faint companions near bright stars, but current ground-based adaptive optics instruments are limited by their sensitivity and angular resolution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach that combines the capabilities of a large telescope and a smaller one to achieve high-contrast imaging. By utilizing a small telescope to measure the star's speckle pattern and then subtracting it from the combined image, we can significantly enhance the contrast and angular resolution. Our simulations demonstrate that this technique can achieve a contrast of 10^-7 at 0.2 arcseconds with a 30-meter telescope and a 1.5-meter telescope, making it feasible to detect Earth-like planets around nearby stars.

This study develops a new model for the short-term interest rate by combining two independent Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, resulting in a non-negative diffusion process. The model's parameters are estimated using a maximum likelihood approach, and its performance is evaluated through a simulation-based analysis.

We have developed a comprehensive framework for analyzing neutrino oscillation experiments, specifically designed to investigate the presence of sterile neutrinos. This framework is built upon the concept of a likelihood function, which is then used to create a versatile tool for comparing different experiments. This tool is applied to the analysis of the MiniBooNE experiment, which has shown intriguing results that could be explained by sterile neutrinos.

In meta-analyses, researchers often use cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators to account for correlations among effect sizes from the same study. However, these estimators can be unreliable when the number of studies is small, leading to inaccurate results. To address this issue, we propose a new estimator that combines the cluster-robust approach with shrinkage, resulting in more precise estimates of variance. This estimator is based on a shrinkage framework and is shown to outperform existing methods through simulation studies.

A new method for simulating particle sediment interactions in fluid dynamics is introduced, which involves extending the time it takes for particles to collide. This technique allows for a more efficient simulation of particle movement and fluid turbulence, which is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments. The results show that stretching the collision time has a significant impact on particle movement and turbulence, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. The proposed method is also found to be consistent with previous research on particle movement and fluid dynamics.

We've developed a new approach to analyze the Unruh/Hawking radiation process, which allows us to demonstrate that the radiation's energy originates from the gravitational field rather than the black hole itself. This is achieved by applying a novel method to calculate the energy-momentum tensor of the quantum field, which involves using a specific type of Green function. This method enables us to derive the energy-momentum tensor in a straightforward manner, which can then be used to calculate the energy flux at the event horizon. This approach also allows us to calculate the energy flux in the case of a black hole with a time-dependent mass, which is a significant advancement in the field.

We examine the transverse momentum broadening of partons in the context of the Color Glass Condensate model, focusing on the impact of the saturation scale on this phenomenon. Our analysis reveals that the broadening effect is significantly influenced by the saturation scale, with the impact being more pronounced for gluons than for quarks.
We establish a new criterion for determining when two positive integers are relatively prime, which is based on the properties of their Fibonacci and Lucas number representations.

In high-performance computing systems, non-volatile memories are increasingly used to ensure fault tolerance. However, the reliability of these memories is compromised by the presence of bit flips, which can be mitigated through error correction techniques. This research focuses on the development of a novel, efficient error correction method for non-volatile memories, which is based on a probabilistic approach. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing the number of bit flips and improving the reliability of non-volatile memories.

To effectively manage intricate information, humans rely on hierarchical structures, which are also employed in various applications such as file systems, databases, and knowledge graphs. This paper presents a novel approach to automatically generating hierarchical structures from unstructured data, specifically by creating a hierarchical representation of knowledge graphs. Our method involves an iterative process that utilizes a neural network to learn the hierarchical structure, which is then refined through a self-supervised learning technique. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

We've developed a new method to calculate the escape probability in complex three-body systems, which is based on the concept of a 'leakage rate' and is applicable to a wide range of non-hierarchical systems. Our approach is validated by comparing it to numerical simulations and is found to be consistent with the predictions of the 'leakage rate' theory. Furthermore, we've applied our method to study the escape probability in various three-body systems, including those with a massive central body and those with equal masses, and have found that our results are in good agreement with the predictions of the 'leakage rate' theory.

We've developed a comprehensive model to analyze the suppression of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons in high-energy nuclear collisions. This model takes into account the effects of color screening and recombination, and is applied to data from the LHC and RHIC experiments. Our results show that the suppression of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons is influenced by the size of the medium, the temperature of the medium, and the recombination process.

We establish a hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic, which facilitates the development of a hyperdoctrine-based semantics for the logic. This framework is then utilized to demonstrate the completeness of the logic.

Regression testing is a crucial process in software development, aimed at detecting unintended changes in software behavior resulting from modifications. To facilitate this, we have developed a novel approach that leverages the power of deep learning to automatically identify relevant test cases for regression testing. Our method involves training a neural network to predict the likelihood of a test case being affected by a code change, thereby enabling the selection of the most pertinent test cases for regression testing.

Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled the development of predictive models for suicidal ideation using Electronic Health Records (EHR). However, these models often overlook the potential of incorporating Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) records, which capture real-time patient experiences. This study aims to investigate the impact of integrating EMA data on the accuracy of predicting suicidal ideation from EHR data. We conducted a comprehensive analysis using data from 100 participants, comparing the performance of models trained on EHR data alone to those trained on combined EHR and EMA data. Our results demonstrate that models trained on combined data outperform those trained on EHR data alone, achieving a 10% increase in accuracy. Furthermore, we found that models trained on combined data are more robust to variations in data collection methods. Our findings suggest that integrating EMA data can significantly enhance the accuracy of predicting suicidal ideation and provide valuable insights for future research in this area.

Our findings reveal that the synchrotron component of X-ray emissions exhibits an average polarization of 10.5% with a standard deviation of 2.5%. Our results also show that the synchrotron component of X-ray emissions exhibits a higher polarization than the thermal component, which is consistent with the expected behavior. We establish a lower limit for the maximum value of $k$ in Erdős's conjecture, which states that for any set of $n$ positive integers, there exists a subset of size $k$ with distinct subset sums. This lower limit is $k \geqslant c\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$, where $c$ is a constant greater than 1.

Our research focuses on the behavior of sound velocity in dense matter, particularly in the context of quark matter. We have developed a model that incorporates the effects of quark mass and color superconductivity, and we have found that the sound velocity decreases as density increases, eventually approaching zero at extremely high densities. This behavior is consistent with the observed properties of quark matter and provides a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of dense matter in neutron stars.

We investigate the optimal use of squeezed and displaced number states for estimating parameters in a specific type of optical system. By applying the quantum Fisher information, we determine the best initial state for maximizing sensitivity. Our analysis reveals that the optimal strategy involves using a squeezed state with a specific displacement, which can be achieved through a straightforward method.

A novel method for skeletonizing gas-liquid interfaces is introduced, which is based on the concept of a signed distance function. This method is applied to a wide range of interface shapes, including those with complex geometries, and is demonstrated through simulations of various scenarios, such as a single droplet, a droplet on a surface, and a droplet in a confined space.

Influenza A viruses, particularly the H1N1 strain, have been observed to exhibit unique behavior when interacting with surfaces coated in glycans. These viruses, which possess spike proteins, have been found to adhere to these surfaces and undergo a process of self-assembly. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers have developed a computational model that simulates the movement of individual viral components on a glicosylated surface. The model reveals that the viruses' spikes can become trapped in the glycans, leading to a process of self-assembly that is influenced by the viruses' movement and the properties of the surface. The results of the simulations suggest that the viruses' behavior is consistent with experimental observations and that the viruses' spikes play a crucial role in their ability to adhere to and self-assemble on glicosylated surfaces.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of 100 galaxies with distorted disk structures, identified through the SDSS survey, focusing on their optical and infrared properties. Our findings reveal that U-type galaxies exhibit bluer colors and higher star formation rates compared to S-type galaxies. Additionally, we found that U-type galaxies are more likely to be found in the outskirts of galaxy clusters, whereas S-type galaxies are more prevalent in the central regions. Our results also indicate that U-type galaxies are more likely to be found in the outskirts of galaxy clusters, whereas S-type galaxies are more prevalent in the central regions.
This paper proves a Liouville theorem for harmonic functions on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with constant scalar curvature, and also establishes a new characterization of such solitons.

Chiral phonons, which are sound waves with a distinct direction of rotation, have been observed in crystals with a specific atomic arrangement. These rotating phonons can be used to create a new type of device that can manipulate and control the flow of heat. In this study, researchers have developed a theoretical model of a chiral phonon system that can be used to create a heat rectifier. The model consists of a rotating crystal structure with a specific atomic arrangement, which allows for the creation of phonons that can be used to create a heat rectifier. The results of the study show that the heat rectifier can be used to create a new type of device that can manipulate and control the flow of heat.

We have developed a new approach to calculate Born effective charges in insulators, which are essential for understanding piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties. Our method involves using the Hellmann-Feynman theorem to derive a formula for calculating these charges, which can be expressed as a sum of two components: one related to the change in the ground state wavefunction and another related to the change in the Hamiltonian. To simplify the calculation, we have developed a technique that allows us to compute the first component using a single excited state, which can be obtained through the use of the Bethe-Salpeter equation. This approach has been successfully applied to a series of materials, including BaTiO3, PbTiO3, and LiNbO3, and our results are in good agreement with previous studies.

We've developed a theoretical framework to analyze thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence, which is based on the Navier-Stokes equation with added thermal noise. This framework is applicable to both periodic and non-periodic domains, and it's shown that the Kolmogorov length is the key factor in determining the significance of thermal effects.

A three-dimensional topological insulator exhibits time-reversal symmetry, which is characterized by a unique property where the product of the time-reversal operator and the Hamiltonian at the Fermi level is equivalent to the negative of the Hamiltonian. This is in contrast to a three-dimensional topological superconductor, which exhibits a distinct property where the time-reversal operator and the Hamiltonian at the Fermi level are equivalent. We demonstrate that a three-dimensional topological insulator can be transformed into a topological superconductor through the application of a specific pairing potential, which is a pairing potential that is invariant under time-reversal symmetry. This is in contrast to a pairing potential that is not invariant under time-reversal symmetry, which can be used to transform a three-dimensional topological insulator into a topological superconductor with a distinct property.

We investigate the delayed nonlinearity in a system of two coupled oscillators, 
where the time delay is periodically varied. Our findings reveal that this 
modulation can significantly enhance the system's synchronization capabilities. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can be effectively utilized 
to control the system's chaotic behavior.

We introduce a novel sound and complete denotational framework for a functional programming language, incorporating a probabilistic interpretation of its core syntax. This framework is underpinned by an adequacy theorem, which we establish, and we also demonstrate that it can be adapted to a probabilistic PCF variant.

In software design mining, the process of extracting design information from source code is a key area of study. This paper presents a novel approach to design mining that leverages the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate Java class diagrams from code snippets. The proposed method, called LLM-CD, utilizes the LLMs' ability to produce Java class diagrams in a concise format, which can then be converted into visual representations using the Graphviz tool. The results of our experiments demonstrate that LLM-CD is effective in producing accurate Java class diagrams, with a high degree of similarity to the original designs.

A new model for dark energy and dark matter is presented, where gravity's origin is attributed to the interaction between the Higgs field and a scalar field, with the latter's dynamics governed by a specific potential. This model's predictions are consistent with the observed acceleration of the universe and the Hubble constant, with the dark energy and dark matter components being linked to the scalar field's kinetic and potential energy, respectively.

Proximal methods are a popular approach for tackling nonsmooth optimization problems, and they can be viewed as a specific case of the general inexact proximal point algorithm. This paper presents a new inexact proximal point algorithm that accommodates a broad class of inexact proximal methods, and it establishes a convergence rate of O(1/k) for the algorithm's merit function under mild assumptions. This result is then applied to derive a convergence rate of O(1/k) for the algorithm's merit function under mild assumptions.
